finding: Row 2's mutant was BUILT and RUN and the row's assertion is never red. I prototyped floor_by_section twice against the real engine (correct: bucket engine.FloorIndexRows(text, engine.FloorAnchorOf(text)) rows whose TextSHA != "" by row.Anchor; mutant: iterate the same uncut rows but call anchorOf(j) with j the 1-based position among UNCUT units). Measured on the fixture the row's own precondition prescribes — a cut unit positioned before a section change — correct = {§1:1, §2:2, §3:1} sum 4, mutant = {§1:2, §2:2} sum 4. On a two-cut variant: correct {§1:1,§2:1,§3:2} sum 4, mutant {§1:2,§2:2} sum 4. On spec/1.0.1.md itself (87 index rows, 62 uncut, 25 cut): correct {§0:2,§1:3,§2:21,§3:6,§4:5,§5:14,§6:11} sum 62, mutant {§0:2,§1:8,§2:22,§3:13,§4:13,§5:4} sum 62. The sum is invariant under ANY anchor misassignment, because every uncut unit still receives exactly one anchor and anchorOf(j) is never out of range for j <= the unit count. So the precondition was never what was wrong — round 3 moved the fixture when the defect is in the assertion. This is the third consecutive round in which row 2 dies.

resolved.evidence: floor_by_section is dropped from the release, so the row whose mutant could not kill it is gone. The anchor behaviour it was trying to assert moves to spec/backlog/04a-ground-command-friction.md with the six fixtures that found it.

suggestion: Do not repair the precondition again. Replace the assertion: assert floor_by_section KEY-BY-KEY against the uncut rows of engine.FloorIndexRows(text, engine.FloorAnchorOf(text)), so the key set is part of the claim. The minimal red-first form on the cut-before-a-section-change fixture is that floor_by_section carries a key for the LAST section (§3) — the mutant drops it entirely, 3 keys vs 2 — and §2's 'its only claim is that they sum to floor_size' must widen with it, since that sentence is what makes the row untestable.

finding: §1's fenced derivation prints NOTHING under zsh, silently, exit 0 — and zsh is the shell this session's tool calls actually run in. Measured, same clone, same HEAD: `bash -c '<the block>'` prints 17 lines (0.23.0 301 17 ... 1.0.0 90 15); `zsh -c '<the same block>'` prints zero lines and exits 0. Cause, isolated: in the quoted string "$tag:spec/.tp-review/$v/snapshot-round-1.md", zsh parses `$tag:s...` as the `:s/old/new/` parameter modifier. Echoing the expansion under zsh gives `v0.36.0shot-round-1.md`, so every `git show` fails with 128 and the `|| continue` skips every iteration. §4's own shipped rule is 'every fenced command in a spec runs at HEAD and prints something', and this block is green under one interpreter and red under another, so the rule as worded is not a deterministic test — two engineers checking the same file reach opposite verdicts. §7 of the measurements file records this block as 'runs, 17 lines', which is the bash reading only.

resolved.evidence: The block now uses ${tag} and ${v} throughout, which closes zsh's :s history modifier; verified printing 17 rows under bash -c in a fresh clone. Section 4's rule now names bash, and measurements section 10 carries the transcript.

suggestion: Two changes, both testable. In §1, quote the revision separately — `git show "${tag}:spec/.tp-review/${v}/snapshot-round-1.md"` (braces terminate the parameter, so the colon is literal in zsh too) — and confirm by running the block under both `bash -c` and `zsh -c` and asserting both print 17 lines. In §4, name the interpreter in the rule ('runs under bash at HEAD and prints something'), so 'runs' has one meaning; a rule whose verdict depends on the reader's login shell is the class of defect the rule exists to catch.

finding: "It is what the emission's own resolver returns, so every reason a role can be absent at round 1 is already reflected in it; `internal/engine/skipped.go` enumerates those reasons" is false for `no-spec-change`, which is one of the five reasons that very file enumerates (skipped.go:12-20). Measured: a probe spec whose frontmatter appends the focus entry "Check §9.9 only" to `architect`, diffed against a baseline differing only in §1 — round 1, `--no-state`, no round 2 anywhere — gives `prompts: ['architect','ax-economist','implementer','tester']` without `--diff-from` and `prompts: ['ax-economist','implementer','tester']`, `skipped: [{'role':'architect','reason':'no-spec-change'}]` with it. internal/cli/review.go's filter is guarded on `diffFrom != ""` alone, not on the round, and it runs AFTER resolveRolePanel — so the emission's role ids are the resolver's set minus a diff-derived subtraction that lint provably cannot make, for the reason §5 Non-Goal 8 itself gives ("lint has no diff"). §6 row 3's SHALL — `review_panel` equal to the emission's role ids for every spec in this repository — is therefore falsified by an invocation rather than by a spec, and no fixture in the repository can protect it.

resolved.evidence: Sentence deleted. Section 2 now states no sentence about runtime behaviour at all.

suggestion: Scope the claim to the invocation as well as the round: `review_panel` equals the role ids of a round-1 emission taken WITHOUT `--diff-from`. Then say that `no-spec-change` is the one enumerated reason lint cannot reflect, and why — which is a stronger statement than the current "every reason", and is the one a reader can act on. §6 row 3 needs the same qualifier or its mutant is not the discriminator it claims.

finding: "`cut` carries the same split" is false, and the split it points at does not exist. The paragraph builds a live/frozen pair for `floor_size`: lint's live count against "the `floor_size` in `tp review`'s `ungrounded` envelope (`internal/engine/groundadvisory.go`)". Measured at HEAD: that envelope is exactly `{"round":1,"undispositioned":1,"floor_size":1}` — it carries NO `cut`, and GroundAdvisory (groundadvisory.go:21-29) has no such field. `tp ground`'s own emission envelope (groundResult, internal/cli/ground.go:41-50) also carries no `cut`: its keys are spec, round, snapshot, floor, output_path, floor_size, carried, prompt. The only `cut` tp emits today is groundStatusResult.Cut in `tp ground --status` (keys measured: by_verdict, cut, dispositioned, emitted, off_floor, reader_added, round, spec), a different command's envelope — and that same envelope reports the uncut count under the name `emitted`, not `floor_size`.

resolved.evidence: Sentence deleted. The envelope claim was false and is not replaced; the floor_size name clash is routed to REFERENCE.md via section 4's documentation task.

suggestion: Say where the frozen `cut` actually lives (`tp ground --status`) rather than asserting parity with the ungrounded envelope, or drop the sentence. A reader who meets lint's `cut` and then looks for its counterpart in the envelope §2 just named finds no key at all, which is the exact confusion the paragraph was written to prevent.

finding: `floor_by_section` is the only one of the four fields that is unbounded in size and the only one whose row states no agent decision it feeds. Measured: rendered as tp's 2-space pretty JSON, the map costs ~149 bytes at 7 distinct numbered anchors (spec/1.0.1.md's shape), ~1,245 at 69 (spec/0.1.0.md) and ~1,641 at 91 (spec/0.23.0.md) — 12% of that file's current 13,425-byte lint output — and ~17.5 KB summed over the 66 specs under spec/ and spec/backlog/. The other three are O(1): two ints and a 4-element list. Against that cost the section offers only an arithmetic identity with a field in the same object ('its only claim is that they sum to `floor_size`'), while §1 says tp makes no judgement and Non-Goal 2 declines to claim seeing any of this changes what an author writes. That is exactly the test that removed `spec_bytes` (arithmetic tp's prompts do not support) and `floor_figure_share` (could not discriminate) — a third field fails it and survived.

resolved.evidence: Field dropped. Two roles reached the same conclusion independently and its only test was refuted; spec/undecided.md carries the measurement and the reopen condition.

suggestion: Either state the decision the split feeds — the obvious one being 'which section to split', which is a real author action the total cannot support — and say so in the row, or cut the field to three and put it in `spec/undecided.md` with the reopening condition, as §2's own two dropped fields were.

finding: §2 requires `review_panel` to be "what the emission's own resolver returns" AND requires lint to report an empty panel and exit 0 when a spec deactivates every reviewer. Both cannot hold: the emission's resolver is `resolveRolePanel` (internal/cli/role_panel.go:83), and on that input it never returns — line 117-119 calls `refuseEmptyPhase`, which is `output.Error(ExitUsage, ...)` + `os.Exit(2)`. Measured on a fixture whose frontmatter sets enabled:false for all four reviewers: `tp review` exits 2 with "every reviewers role is deactivated by this spec"; `tp lint` exits 0 today only because it does not call the resolver. So the implementer must either (a) reimplement resolution inside lint from ResolveActiveCorpus + ResolveOverrideFocus + DropDisabledRoles, which is the second derivation §2's floor_size paragraph forbids for every other field, or (b) split `resolveRolePanel` into a pure resolver plus the two §2.5 refusals — a change to a function §2.5 requires both review and audit to call ahead of every write. §2 does not say which, and the choice decides whether §6 row 3's mutant is even applicable.

resolved.evidence: New section 7 makes the resolver split a requirement: pure resolution plus a refusing wrapper, review keeps the wrapper, lint calls the pure function. It is a task of its own and a dependency of the review_panel task.

suggestion: State which of the two the release takes. If (b), name it as its own task ahead of the review_panel task: extract the resolution from the refusals in role_panel.go, keep review's and audit's call sites refusing exactly as now, and have lint call the pure half.

finding: §4 says "Four are new; a fifth already shipped and is named here only as precedent, not as work." The list under that sentence has SEVEN bullets: six new rules (a number does not live in a spec / every fenced command runs at HEAD / the body is ADR-shaped / write a test row's mutant before its assertion / a grading brief names the record / a check prototype states how it judged its findings) and one precedent bullet (a finding leaves a round as a spec change or a --resolve disposition). So "four" is wrong by two and "a fifth" names the seventh item. Counted at HEAD from spec/1.0.1.md lines 133, 136, 139, 141, 147, 150 and 153.

resolved.evidence: The count is gone. Section 4 now derives it from the bullet list itself: the new rules are the bullet count less one, the last bullet being the precedent.

suggestion: Replace the count with the shape the list already has — "the bullets below are the new rules; the last is named as precedent, not as work" — or state six and one. A count of a list in the same paragraph as the list is the cheapest possible instance of this repository's most-repeated defect class, and §4 is the section that ships the rule against it.

finding: Non-Goal 8's replacement blocker is refuted by one run, exactly as its predecessor was. It says "an audit round reads a *change*: `tp audit` needs a changed-file set and exits 4 without one, and lint has no diff." Measured: in a pristine `git clone --no-hardlinks` of this repo with `git status --porcelain` returning ZERO lines, `tp audit spec/1.0.1.md` exits **0** and prints `324 files changed, auditing first 50 — name the rest with --affected-files`. `tp audit spec/1.0.1.md --affected-files ""` is the same: exit 0, same 324. tp audit auto-detects its set from git and needs nothing from the operator, so "needs a changed-file set" is false and "exits 4 without one" is not the default path (the exit-4 sinks in internal/cli/audit.go are exitAuditNoFiles under --affected-from-tasks and a resolution error, not an absent set). The "lint has no diff" half then blocks nothing that tp does not already do without a supplied diff.

resolved.evidence: The derivation is gone rather than replaced. A Non-Goal that is out of scope needs no reason, and this one had two refuted in two rounds.

suggestion: Either name the blocker that survives a run, or drop the derivation and state the non-goal flat ("deferred; no audit-side counterpart ships in this release"). This Non-Goal has now had two derivations refuted by a single run each; a third derivation is a worse bet than no derivation. If a blocker is wanted, the honest candidate is that the audited FILE SET is not a property of the spec — auto-detection resolves against a git base, so lint would report a panel keyed on the caller's working tree rather than on the document, which is what §2 says review_panel must not be.

finding: Row 3's "for every spec in this repository" test has no runnable shape as written. (a) Run in-repo: a round-1 `tp review` emission writes the snapshot and state.json, and 40 spec state directories already exist, so 66 emissions move state that `scripts/check-suite-state.sh` hashes before and after the suite; CLAUDE.md forbids `--no-state` as the escape. (b) Relocate: `relocatedSpecAtRoundOne` (internal/cli/sandbox_helpers_test.go:101-112) copies only the spec body, so `DiscoverTPDir` finds no `.tp/` and the panel falls back to the embedded default — measured, a relocated copy of spec/1.0.1.md emits ['implementer','tester','architect'] against the repo's ['architect','ax-economist','implementer','tester']. Under (b) the parity holds trivially and the user corpus, which row 3 calls the assertion, is never exercised. (c) The quantifier has a counterexample regardless: `tp review spec/0.28.0.md` exits 4 ("review round budget exhausted: 4 rounds recorded with a cap of 4") and emits no prompts at all — even with `--no-state --round 1` — so no round-1 emission exists for it.

resolved.evidence: Row replaced. The repository corpus is not the fixture; row 2 now builds a temporary corpus in which exactly one role declares domains.

suggestion: Name the helper the row needs: a relocation that copies `.tp/reviewers/*.json` into the temp tree alongside the spec, so the corpus travels and every relocated spec is at round 1. And state what the test does with a spec whose emission is refused (skip with the reason recorded, or exclude the state-dir-bearing specs from the universal).

finding: Row 3's universal ('for every spec in this repository') is not evaluable, in three separate ways, each measured. (a) A round-1 emission cannot be produced for 17 of the 66 specs: they already carry at least one recorded review-round file, so their next emission is not round 1 and forcing one means deleting recorded state. (b) `tp review spec/0.28.0.md` exits 4 with 'review round budget exhausted: 4 rounds recorded with a cap of 4 and not converged' and emits no prompts at all, so 'the emission's role ids' has no value there — 65 of 66 parsed. (c) The comparison is FALSE where it is evaluable: 13 of the 65 emissions carry `regression` in prompts[], while §2 states lint's round-1 review_panel excludes regression because the emitter appends it only from a round with a baseline. Two engineers write contradictory tests — one compares against the current emission and gets 13 mismatches, one deletes state to force round 1 and mutates the repository. A fourth cost: 66 emissions write 66 spec state directories, which is exactly what scripts/check-suite-state.sh exists to fail on.

resolved.evidence: Same replacement. The universal over the repository is gone, and measurements section 12 records why it was unevaluable.

suggestion: Quantify the row over a bounded, relocated fixture set rather than over 'this repository': copy N specs plus their .tp-review/<base> into t.TempDir() (the relocatedSpec pattern CLAUDE.md already prescribes for this hazard), emit round 1 there, and compare. State in the row that the emission compared against is a round-1 one produced in the relocated tree, and that regression is expected absent because that round has no baseline.

finding: "The count `internal/cli/ground.go` performs today moves into `internal/engine` as an exported function and both callers use it, so lint adds no third derivation" rests on there being one derivation today. There are two. groundFloorSize (internal/cli/ground.go:443-450) counts index rows with a non-empty TextSHA; GroundCoverageOf (internal/engine/groundcoverage.go:65-72) opens with `for _, r := range floor { if r.TextSHA == "" { continue }; emitted[r.ID] = true }` — the same predicate over the same rows, and its result is what `tp review`'s advisory publishes as `floor_size` (groundadvisory.go:84) and what `tp ground --status` publishes as `emitted`. So after the move engine holds the new exported function AND GroundCoverageOf's inline loop, and lint is the third caller of a quantity tp already spells three ways in three envelopes (`floor_size`, `floor_size`, `emitted`).

resolved.evidence: Sentence deleted. The table's derived-by column names engine.FloorUnits and says nothing about how many other derivations exist.

suggestion: Either say the move folds GroundCoverageOf's loop into the same exported function — which is the version that makes "no third derivation" true — or drop the count and say only that lint and ground call one exported function. As written the sentence promises an invariant the described change does not establish.

finding: "a malformed role file exits 3 in both, because lint already loads the corpus" is false for an AUDITOR role file, and the reason §2 gives is why. Measured in a clone at HEAD: with `.tp/auditors/zz-broken.json` holding non-JSON, `tp lint <spec>` exits 3 and `tp review <spec>` exits **0**; with the identical file under `.tp/reviewers/`, both exit 3; with neither, both exit 0. lint loads BOTH phases — lintRoleCorpusOrAbort (internal/cli/lint.go:39-47) iterates `PhaseReviewers, PhaseAuditors` — while `tp review` calls resolveRolePanel(specPath, PhaseReviewers) only, whose own comment says the abort "aborts its own phase (§3.6, exit 3) and never the other one". So lint loading the corpus is precisely what makes the two commands disagree, rather than what makes them agree.

resolved.evidence: Sentence deleted. Section 7 carries the two commands' exit codes as a table, and explicitly does not pin the malformed-auditor row because the release does not change it.

suggestion: Narrow it to the phase: "a malformed REVIEWER role file exits 3 in both; a malformed auditor role file exits 3 in lint and is invisible to `tp review`." That is a sharper statement about lint's edges and it is the one a test can pin.

finding: Four of §2's stated behaviours have no row in §6, and three of the four are already runnable today, so each could be a red-first test rather than a sentence. (1) `cut` is one of the four fields the release adds and no row asserts its value — rows 1-3 assert floor_size, floor_by_section and review_panel, and row 1 uses cut only as a precondition. §2 spends a paragraph ('Why `cut` is reported at all') on a number nothing checks. (2) The live-vs-frozen divergence, which is the section's newest and most disputed content, is measurable now: on a copy of this spec, emit a round, append three gradeable units, and the live floor is 65 while `tp review`'s ungrounded.floor_size stays 62 — no row covers it. (3) The all-reviewers-deactivated edge: measured, `tp review` exits 2 with 'every reviewers role is deactivated by this spec: architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester' while `tp lint` exits 0 on the same file. (4) The malformed-role-file edge: measured, `tp lint` and `tp review` both exit 3 with 'invalid role JSON'. §2's no-further-prose-repair rule makes rows the only channel left for these claims, and they have none.

resolved.evidence: Every field now carries a pinned-by column naming its test. A behaviour claim without a test name is no longer in the section.

suggestion: Add rows, not sentences. cut: on a fixture with a known cut count, assert cut == len(FloorIndexRows) - floor_size, mutant = report zero for a spec with cut units. Divergence: emit, append units, assert lint's floor_size != the ungrounded envelope's, with the two measured integers in the row. The two exit edges are regression guards on behaviour that already holds — assert the exit code and the message, mutant = lint refusing (exit 2) alongside review.

finding: The section adds four fields to `tp lint` and never says whether any of them survives `--compact` or `--quiet`, and the measured default is that none can be suppressed. At HEAD, `tp lint spec/1.0.1.md`, the same with `--compact`, and the same with `--quiet` all return 3,077 bytes, the same seven top-level keys and all ten info-severity findings; `internal/cli/lint.go` contains no reference to either flag. So 'no config field' is bought by making four fields unconditional on every lint of every spec forever, and the unbounded one (`floor_by_section`) is the one an agent most often does not need. The same struct already carries the precedent for the fix — `StructuredElements` is tagged `json:"structured_elements,omitempty"` at internal/cli/lint.go:25.

resolved.evidence: Section 2 now states it: the three are siblings of structured_elements, emitted on every invocation, and lint varies its payload by neither --compact nor --quiet today.

suggestion: State the `--compact` contract in §2: at minimum the two scalars and the panel survive `--compact` and `floor_by_section` does not. If instead all four are unconditional, say so and say why, so the choice is a recorded decision rather than an omission — and add a test row for it, since nothing in §6 pins the flag behaviour.

finding: The table row and the edge-case paragraph define `review_panel` incompatibly. Row 4 says it is "the role ids `tp review`'s own resolver returns"; the paragraph says "a spec that deactivates every reviewer makes `tp review` exit 2 while lint reports an empty `review_panel` and exits 0". That resolver is resolveRolePanel (internal/cli/role_panel.go:83-121), and BOTH refusals live inside it: `if len(disabled) > 0 && len(roles) == 0 { refuseEmptyPhase(phase, disabled) }` at line 117, and the exit-3 corpus abort at line 89. Measured: on a spec deactivating architect, ax-economist, implementer and tester, `tp review` exits 2 with `every reviewers role is deactivated by this spec: architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester` and `tp lint` exits 0 — so on the exact input the paragraph is about, "tp review's own resolver" RETURNS nothing at all. The row's definition cannot be implemented as written and also satisfy the paragraph.

resolved.evidence: Both definitions are gone; section 7 states the split that makes one definition possible.

suggestion: Define `review_panel` as what the resolution produces MINUS the emission-only refusals — the resolver's roles list, not the resolver's process — and say so in the row rather than only in the paragraph. That also settles what lint does on the exit-3 half, where §2 does want the refusal inherited.

finding: `review_panel`'s rationale defends the cheap half of its case and never states the expensive one. The list-vs-count argument is worth 73 bytes: `"review_panel":["architect","ax-economist","implementer","tester"]` is 96 bytes of pretty JSON against 23 for `"review_panel": 4`. The field's actual saving is that today the ONLY way to learn a spec's round-1 panel is to emit the prompts — measured at HEAD in an rsync copy, `tp review spec/1.0.1.md --no-state` returns 22,181 bytes to deliver four role ids, and without `--no-state` it also writes a round. So the field replaces 22,181 bytes and a state write with 96 bytes and none, a 231x reduction on the one quantity of the four that has no cheap path at all. §2 argues the 73-byte point and omits the 22,085-byte one, which is the strongest AX case in the release.

resolved.evidence: Section 1 now carries the case, with the byte counts in measurements section 11. The list-versus-count argument stays but is no longer the case for shipping.

suggestion: Keep the list-vs-count sentence and add the measurement: the panel is otherwise reachable only through an emission, so this field is the only one of the four that removes a round-trip rather than reordering when one is paid.

finding: §2 does not say which text lint derives the floor from, and the two candidates disagree. `runLint` already holds `lines`, but `parseSpecFile` (internal/cli/lint.go:147-172) runs them through `engine.BlankFrontmatterLines` at line 164, so a spec's frontmatter reaches lint as blank lines; `tp ground` derives its floor from the raw file bytes (internal/cli/ground.go:334, 366). `floorBlocks` splits on blank lines, so blanked frontmatter inserts block boundaries that the raw text does not have, and on any spec with frontmatter lint's `floor_size` and ground's would differ. Row 1's test cannot catch this: 0 of the 66 markdown files under spec/ carry frontmatter, so the fixture that would separate the two readings does not exist in the corpus the row is run over.

resolved.evidence: Row 1 now names both invocations exactly: tp lint <spec> against tp ground <spec> --units, equal to the latter's line count.

suggestion: State that lint re-reads the file with os.ReadFile and derives the floor from the same bytes tp ground uses, and give row 1 a fixture that carries frontmatter so the two readings are separated.

finding: §2 names four quantities and never says where they land in `tp lint`'s payload. `lintResult` (internal/cli/lint.go:18-26) has seven keys today (file, errors, warnings, info, frontmatter, findings, structured_elements) and `newLintCmd` (lint.go:49-56) registers no flags at all, so there is no `--compact` to strip anything. Unanswered and each a coin-flip an implementer must make alone: top-level keys or one nested object; present always or omitted when the floor is empty; `floor_by_section` as an object keyed by anchor or an array of {anchor,count}; `review_panel` before or after `frontmatter`, given that both describe the same resolution. Rows 1 and 3 refer to `floor_size` and `review_panel` as if they were wire keys, which makes the shape load-bearing for the tests, not only for readers. Grounding round 1 recorded this gap and no round has closed it.

resolved.evidence: Section 2 now names the payload position and the flag behaviour.

suggestion: Add the four keys to the lintResult shape in §2 — names, nesting and presence rule — as a payload sketch rather than prose, so the row-1 and row-3 tests can assert on them.

finding: §2 states "a malformed role file exits 3 in both, because lint already loads the corpus". Measured at HEAD on an rsync copy: with .tp/auditors/go-safety.json replaced by `{ this is not json`, `tp lint spec/1.0.1.md` exits 3 and `tp review spec/1.0.1.md --no-state` exits 0. The two commands do not load the same corpus — `lintRoleCorpusOrAbort` (internal/cli/lint.go:39-47) loops over BOTH PhaseReviewers and PhaseAuditors, while `runReview` calls `resolveRolePanel(specPath, engine.PhaseReviewers)` only (internal/cli/review.go:569). So the claim holds for a reviewer-phase malformation and is false for an auditor-phase one, and an implementer writing the error-path task from this sentence would pin the wrong behaviour.

resolved.evidence: Section 7's table carries it, and says the malformed-auditor asymmetry is deliberately not pinned by this release.

suggestion: Scope the sentence to the reviewer phase, or say that lint's exit-3 surface is deliberately wider than review's because lint validates both corpora.

finding: §2's "The count internal/cli/ground.go performs today moves into internal/engine as an exported function and both callers use it, so lint adds no third derivation" does not produce the single derivation it claims. After the move there are still two implementations of the same cut predicate inside internal/engine: the moved counter (today `groundFloorSize`, ground.go:443-451, `r.TextSHA != ""`) and `GroundCoverageOf`'s emitted map (internal/engine/groundcoverage.go:66-72, `r.TextSHA == ""` → continue), and the second one is what publishes the SAME JSON name through `GroundAdvisory.FloorSize` (groundadvisory.go:26-28, 84) — the very collision §2's paragraph above it exists to disambiguate, and the one spec/1.0.1-measurements.md §9.2 claim 1 names. The implementer needs to know whether the move task must also rewrite GroundCoverageOf onto the exported predicate or deliberately leave it.

resolved.evidence: The claim about the move is gone. The requirement is that lint derives floor_size from engine.FloorUnits; how many other callers derive it is the implementation task's concern, not a spec claim.

suggestion: Say which call sites the exported function replaces. If GroundCoverageOf is out of scope, say so, because the sentence as written reads as a claim of uniqueness over a set nobody enumerated.

finding: §3 reads as this release's work but the repair is already in the tree, 24 commits behind HEAD. `65406160 fix(lint): vague-language skips fenced blocks and inline spans, like its four siblings` is an ancestor of HEAD (verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`), and its parent is 9297dd2b, the commit §3 names. blankInlineCode and the fence loop are present in internal/engine/vague.go at HEAD (lines 43-61 and 77-87). I ran §3's fenced command in a throwaway clone and it prints `9297dd2b: 2` then `65406160: 0`, so the assertion holds — but the reader cannot tell from §3 that "this release repairs one rule" describes a commit rather than a plan, while §4's neighbouring framing ("The rules are the release, as much as the code is") is forward-looking. This matters to the dependency order the prompt asks about: if §3's code has landed, the only new implementation this release carries is §2's four lint fields, and §6 rows 4-7 are tests of behaviour that already ships.

resolved.evidence: Section 3 now says it: the repair is at 65406160 with tests for rows 4 through 7, and row 8 is the only outstanding work.

suggestion: State it: the rule change landed at 65406160; what §3 still owes is the eight rows of §6. That also removes the reader's ambiguity about whether a §3 test failing means a regression or an unimplemented requirement.

finding: 'Write a test row's mutant before its assertion, and drop the row if the mutant cannot make it red' is an ordering rule about the author's private process, and the artifact records no ordering — a table whose rows were written in either order is byte-identical. So the rule cannot be followed-and-checked at the moment of writing; it can only be adjudicated by a later round. §4's own text supplies the evidence: rows were dropped 'in every one of this spec's grading rounds' and one survived two, meaning the rule was enforced by the rounds, not by the author who had already adopted it. A rule an agent can only be judged against afterwards costs rounds rather than saving them, which is precisely the economy this release exists to improve. The neighbouring rule 'every fenced command runs at HEAD and prints something' is the contrast: it is a property of the artifact, so it was applied mechanically before a round and caught two defects.

resolved.evidence: The rule now requires a row to quote its fixture and both counts, at HEAD and under the mutant, which is checkable by reading the row.

suggestion: Restate it as a checkable property of the table rather than of the author: 'every row names a mutant, and no row's mutant is one another row in the same table already kills.' That is decidable by reading the finished table, is the thing the ordering was for, and is what §6's rows 5-8 already demonstrate by construction.

finding: The one §4 rule with demonstrated mechanical yield ships as prose. 'Every fenced command in a spec runs at `HEAD` and prints something' was applied mechanically before round 3 of this spec's own grounding and caught two defects before a grading token was spent — §4 says so itself. The mechanism to ship it as a check already exists and is already in use: `.tp/config.json` carries a registered `workflow.checks` entry (`code-citation-drift`, `python3 scripts/check-spec-code-citations.py …`), and this round's own emission ran it and reported `exit_code: 1`. Its subject — a fenced command in the spec text — exists in the review phase, which is the condition this repository states for registering a check rather than writing prose. Shipped as SKILL.md prose instead, the rule becomes one every reviewer must re-apply by hand each round, which is the cost the rule was written to remove.

resolved.evidence: Correct, and out of scope. Registering the fenced-command check is a workflow.checks change, and this repository's own rule is that a check is registered only when its subject exists in the phase the check runs in and only after the check itself has been tested. Section 4 gets it as far as prose can: the rule names bash and requires the pre-round step to invoke bash -c. The registration belongs to a release that can test the check.

suggestion: Ship the rule as a registered `workflow.checks` class (`fenced-command-runs`) alongside `code-citation-drift`, with the SKILL.md bullet naming the check rather than restating the rule. If the check is deferred, say in §5 why a rule with two measured catches is not being mechanized, so the decision is recorded rather than implied.

finding: The preamble claims "This file is the first instance of the rule it ships", and §4's first bullet states the rule as "A number does not live in a spec. A reference does … the spec names the artifact and does not quote the figure, and a rationale that cites a figure is a figure." The body does not satisfy it, and the failures are all of one shape — the artifact is named AND the figure is quoted beside it: §2 "Three drafts of this section restated a rule instead … §9 carries the three"; §5 Non-Goal 3 "Six candidates were prototyped … all six were refuted; `spec/undecided.md` carries each measurement"; §4's own fourth bullet "including one that failed twice"; §6 "one survived two rounds because its precondition named the wrong property of its fixture"; §1 "the two within-class correlations have opposite signs", which is a derived result and, by the bullet's last clause, a figure. None of these is a decision in the sense a field count or an exit code is.

resolved.evidence: The rule now draws the line it was missing: a count of a named artifact's own items is a reference in numeral form, a number that is the decision stays, and only a measurement the author's run alone supports leaves.

suggestion: Add the carve-out the file is actually operating under — a count that names its own artifact in the same sentence is a reference, not a figure — and say so in the bullet, so SKILL.md ships the rule the spec obeys rather than one it violates six times. The alternative (deleting the counts) makes §2 and §6 weaker, so the carve-out is the better repair; what is not tenable is shipping the strict form beside a body that breaks it.

finding: §4's rule — 'write a test row's mutant before its assertion, and drop the row if the mutant cannot make it red' — is evidence AGAINST itself in this file, and the evidence is this round's. Three of §6's eight rows (2, 3 and 8) name a mutant, in the required order, that is green on a fixture the row's own precondition permits: row 2's sum survives every anchor misassignment (measured on three fixtures and on this spec), row 3's domain filter is inert on a corpus where no role file declares `domains` (0 domain-mismatch across 65 emissions), and row 8's mutant is green on three of the four siblings its precondition admits. None of the three is a missing mutant; all three are a mutant paired with the wrong fixture or corpus. §6's own preamble already concedes the analogous point about EARS — 'the shape did not prevent it' — and the ordering rule has now failed the same way, in the same table, three times in one round. A rule that ships to users in SKILL.md while its author's own table violates it 3 of 8 times is not yet a rule.

resolved.evidence: Same repair as finding 21: the row must carry its fixture and both counts, which is what makes the rule bind.

suggestion: Strengthen the rule to bind the fixture, since the fixture is where every failure has been: 'a test row states the fixture the mutant was run on and the two counts it produced — the value under HEAD and the value under the mutant. A row that cannot quote both has not been run.' That form is checkable by reading the row, it is what would have caught rows 2, 3 and 8 before emission, and it is the same move CLAUDE.md already records for prose claims — bind the claim to an artifact rather than asserting it.

finding: Non-Goal 2's 'Three of these quantities are already reachable without a round — `tp ground <spec> --units`' is a quantifier over a set the command does not contain, and it understates the release. Measured at HEAD in an rsync copy: `--units` emits exactly three tab-separated columns on every line (unit id, hash, text) — `awk -F'\t' '{print NF}' | sort | uniq -c` returns `62 3` on spec/1.0.1.md and `111 3` on spec/1.0.2.md, no fourth column and no anchor anywhere. So `floor_size` is reachable (the line count, 62). `cut` is reachable only as `max(unit id) - line count` (87 - 62 = 25), an inference about id density over the cut-inclusive population that nothing in the spec or the command's help states. `floor_by_section` is not reachable from that output at all. At most two of the four, not three — and since this sentence is the release's own account of what it does not add, the error makes the release look less earned than the measurement supports. `review_panel` is not reachable from `ground` in any mode.

resolved.evidence: Non-Goal 2 now says floor_size is the reachable one and lint adds the other two.

suggestion: Replace the count with the enumeration the command supports: `floor_size` is `tp ground <spec> --units | wc -l`; `cut` is available from `tp ground <spec> --status`, which needs an emitted round; `floor_by_section` and `review_panel` have no round-free path today. Then the Non-Goal still holds and stops asserting a number.

finding: Row 1 says 'WHEN `tp lint` and `tp ground` run over it', and `tp ground` has three modes that answer differently, so two engineers write different tests. Measured on a copy of this spec: the bare emission `tp ground <spec>` is the ONLY mode whose JSON carries a `floor_size` key (keys: carried, floor, floor_size, output_path, prompt, round, snapshot, spec) and it reports 62; `tp ground <spec> --status` carries no `floor_size` at all — its keys are spec, round, emitted, dispositioned, reader_added, off_floor, cut, by_verdict — and the corresponding number is `emitted`; `tp ground <spec> --units` prints text lines with no JSON, 62 of them. So an engineer reaching for the read-only mode finds no field of that name and must know that `emitted` is the same quantity, while the one mode that does name it WRITES a round — which against a spec in this repository is exactly what scripts/check-suite-state.sh fails on, and what §9.3 of the measurements file warns about for the sibling command.

resolved.evidence: Row 1 now names tp ground <spec> --units explicitly.

suggestion: Name the invocation in the row: '`tp lint <spec>`'s floor_size equals the `floor_size` of `tp ground <spec>`'s emission, taken in a relocated tree'. Adding the relocation to the row is not decoration — without it the test either mutates the repository or is written against --status, whose number §2 says diverges from lint's after an edit.

finding: Row 8 has no test at HEAD, so the §3 task cannot close on existing coverage. internal/engine/vague_fence_test.go holds five tests — SkipsFencedBlocks, SkipsInlineCodeSpans, FixtureWordsAreRealTriggers, StillReportsProse, TreatsUnterminatedFenceLikeItsSiblings — covering rows 4, 5, 6 and 7, and not one of them calls a sibling rule; the only mention of `CheckDuplicateConsecutiveLines` in that file is inside a doc comment. Row 8's assertion is the joint one (the sibling still reports while vague-language does not) and nothing asserts it. The behaviour itself does hold: measured, a two-line fixture repeating "The list covers `appropriate` and `various`." returns exactly one finding, `duplicate-line` at line 6, and zero `vague-language`. So row 8 is a new test to write, not covered work, and its mutant ("blank inline spans for every rule in the file") would make it red.

resolved.evidence: Section 3 now states that row 8 has no test at HEAD and is new work, and that rows 4 through 7 close against existing coverage.

suggestion: Split §3 into two tasks: the shipped repair, which closes with --covered-by naming vague_fence_test.go, and row 8's joint test, which is new work with its own acceptance.

finding: Row 8's stated mutant does not fail row 8 on half of its own justification, so by §6's preamble rule the row does not belong in the table as written. The mutant is "blank inline spans for every rule in the file" and the justification is "a backticked line is still a duplicate and still a broken reference". Built and run: in a clone at HEAD I changed CheckDuplicateConsecutiveLines' `trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(line)` to `strings.TrimSpace(blankInlineCode(line))` — the mutant, applied to the repetition sibling — and linted a fixture holding two consecutive identical lines each reading "The word `appropriate` is named here, not used." HEAD reports `{'duplicate-line': 1}`; the mutant reports `{'duplicate-line': 1}`. The sibling still reports, so the mutant satisfies the row's assertion instead of failing it. This is structural, not fixture-dependent: blankInlineCode is deterministic and length-preserving per line, so two identical lines blank to two identical lines and equality is invariant under it — the same holds for CheckDuplicateParagraphs. Only broken-cross-ref discriminates: measured at HEAD, a backticked `§1.4 step 9` under a §1.4 heading with two numbered items IS reported (line 12 of that fixture, alongside the bare form on line 10), and blanking would remove the ref.

resolved.evidence: Row 8 now names broken-cross-ref, which is the only sibling the mutant kills, and records the measured 1 to 1 invariance of the three duplicate rules.

suggestion: Name the sibling in the row — `broken-cross-ref` — and drop the "still a duplicate" half from both the row and §3's prose that repeats it. §3's principle survives intact; what does not survive is the claim that excluding inline spans in the repetition rules "would be wrong", since it is unobservable there.

finding: §1's fenced command carries `rm -rf /tmp/.tp-review` after `tp ground s.md --units`, a cleanup for a write that does not happen, and the line teaches every reader a cost model for `--units` that Non-Goal 2 then depends on. Measured twice at HEAD with the freshly built binary: (a) in an empty scratch directory holding only `s.md`, `tp ground s.md --units` exits 0 and `find . -type f` afterwards still lists only `./s.md` — nothing created; (b) in an rsync copy of this repository with spec/1.0.1.md edited so the text has moved since round 3, the eleven files under spec/.tp-review/1.0.1/ are md5-identical before and after the call, and no round 4 appears. `--units` writes nothing under either condition. Six bytes of a fenced command are not the cost; the false model is — a reader who takes it at face value budgets a state write for a read-only call, and this repository's grading briefs warn units away from `--units` on exactly that belief.

resolved.evidence: The rm -rf line is gone. tp ground --units was measured twice to write nothing.

suggestion: Drop the `rm -rf` line from the loop and, if the read-only property of `--units` is load-bearing for Non-Goal 2, state it there as a measured fact rather than leaving the fence to imply the opposite.

finding: §1's fenced command carries `rm -rf /tmp/.tp-review` inside the loop, which reads as a cleanup after a write `tp ground --units` performs. It performs none. I ran the command verbatim at HEAD (it prints 17 rows, so §4's "runs and prints something" rule is satisfied) and `/tmp/.tp-review` does not exist afterwards; runGroundUnits (internal/cli/ground.go:470-502) reads the spec, prints, and its doc says it "takes no lock and writes nothing: no round is emitted". §5 Non-Goal 2 asserts the same thing in words — "`tp ground <spec> --units` lists the floor, writes nothing, and §1 of this file uses exactly that path" — so a reader comparing the recipe against the Non-Goal has to run the command to learn which is true.

resolved.evidence: Same removal.

suggestion: Delete the `rm -rf` line. It is the only thing in the file suggesting `--units` writes, and Non-Goal 2 leans on the opposite. (Separately verified and NOT a finding: the `--units | grep -c '^u[0-9]'` count is the uncut population, so §1's derived quantity is the same one §2 calls `floor_size` — measured 1 unit printed against `floor_size: 1`, `cut: 3`, 4 index rows.)

finding: `cut`'s justification names a quantity a single lint cannot produce. 'A rising cut share is a widening blind spot rather than a cheaper round' — *rising* is a round-over-round comparison, and the same section states four paragraphs later that 'Lint has no round.' One `tp lint` yields one share and no baseline, and the release ships no history, no diff and no threshold that would supply one. The field itself is an int and costs nothing, so the defect is in the sentence, not the field: it justifies `cut` by a use the release does not enable, which is the same shape as a speculative field even though the field is cheap.

resolved.evidence: Reworded: the justification now claims only that cut units are a blind spot and that printing the count stops a small floor being read as a cheap round. The trend claim is explicitly the reader's, across two lints.

suggestion: Justify `cut` by what one lint delivers: reported beside `floor_size` it lets an author read the share the arms will drop from a single call, and stops the uncut count being mistaken for the whole population. Leave 'rising' to whatever release supplies a baseline.

finding: Row 4's named mutant is killed by sibling rows in the same table, so the row buys no discrimination the panel does not already have. Row 4's mutant is 'scan every line' — an implementation with no fence and no inline-span exclusion. Row 5's fixture is a vague word inside an inline code span and asserts nothing is reported; row 8's fixture is a vague word inside an inline code span on a line a structural rule also matches. Under 'scan every line' both fixtures report the trigger word, so both rows go red on row 4's mutant. Rows 5, 6, 7 and 8 each name a mutant no sibling kills, and the section argues that explicitly for rows 6 and 7 ('passes rows 4 and 5', 'passes rows 4 and 6'); row 4 is the only row for which the reverse argument is not made and does not hold. Eight rows is eight tests to write and maintain, and this release's own §4 rule is to drop a row whose mutant does not earn it.

resolved.evidence: Row 4 is redundant against row 5's mutant alone, but each of rows 4 through 7 pins a distinct SHALL and the set is chosen so that each mutant passes some siblings and fails exactly one. Dropping row 4 would leave the fenced-block requirement asserted only as a side effect of the inline-span row.

suggestion: Either drop row 4 and let rows 5-8 carry the fence exclusion, or name for row 4 a mutant no other row kills — an implementation that excludes inline spans but not fenced blocks would be one, and it is the natural half-fix the repair could have shipped.

finding: Row 6's parenthetical about its mutant is false, measured. I built the mutant (`inFence = true` instead of the toggle, i.e. skip everything after the first fence opens) and ran tp lint on a fixture with a vague word in prose before the fence and another after it. The row says the mutant 'reports nothing at all'; it reports ONE — the pre-fence occurrence is still scanned and still reported (baseline 2 vague-language findings, mutant 1). The row still goes red on the stated assertion (2 != 1) and its two other claims hold as written — the same mutant leaves rows 4, 5 and 7's fixtures at their baseline counts — so the row belongs in the table. But the mutant-side expectation is what a second engineer would encode, and 'nothing at all' and 'one' are contradictory assertions.

resolved.evidence: Row 6 now carries the measured counts, 2 at HEAD and 1 under the mutant, instead of the false claim that the mutant reports nothing.

suggestion: Replace 'reports nothing at all' with the measured pair — 'reports one of the two, the pre-fence occurrence' — or drop the clause. The row's discriminating power does not depend on it; only the reproducibility of the check does.
